# RequestFox

> RequestFox is a free browser extension for Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox that records every API call a web app makes while you test it, and automatically flags failed (4xx/5xx), slow, duplicate and retried requests, N+1 bursts, GraphQL and JSON-RPC errors returned with a 200 OK, and 401s caused by an expired token. It can replay, mock and export any request, and generate tests and load-test scripts from recorded traffic. It needs no account, has no server, and keeps all captured data on the user's own device. Current version: 2.4.0 (updated 2026-11-04).

Key facts:

- Type: browser extension (Chrome side panel, Firefox sidebar). Price: free, with no paid tier. Source code: MIT licence; repository not public.
- Capture: fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket frames (Socket.IO frames read as events) and Server-Sent Events, across tabs, iframes and popups, including responses served by a service worker. Each call is listed the moment it starts. Live streams (SSE, NDJSON, token streams; read with fetch, XMLHttpRequest or EventSource) show their events as rows while open and keep the newest ones within the body limit, with error events, a missing end marker and long pauses flagged; gRPC-Web and Connect server streams are kept the same way.
- The log: cards or a table (one line per call, sortable, with columns that read a value from each JSON answer), Group by host, and a session Overview (counts, status families, slowest calls, findings by kind, hosts). Up to five requests stay open in Compose at once.
- Detection: failed, slow, duplicate and retried requests; N+1 bursts (paths grouped into templates like /products/{id}/reviews); errors inside a 200 OK (GraphQL, JSON-RPC); 401/403 caused by an expired JWT (decoded locally, times only); API contract drift (a response's JSON shape changing); per-endpoint checks including JSON Schema; GraphQL answers checked against a loaded schema; XPath checks on XML (SOAP) answers. Every finding has a stable code (such as RF-FAILED-5XX) with an offline explanation. Each flagged call links to the user action (click or form submit) that triggered it, and failures are explained in plain words.
- Log table and Overview extras: Add column (a value from each JSON answer by a path) and Columns (show, hide, reorder, up to four answer columns, saved per site); Copy as Markdown (calls named by host and path only) and a Calls over time chart in the Overview.
- Answers: Hex view (offset, hex, ASCII; 32 KB drawn at most) with Copy as base64; a JSON list of objects as a Table with sort and Copy as CSV; a web address in an answer opens as a new request in Compose (Open as request).
- GraphQL in Compose: subscriptions over graphql-transport-ws or graphql-ws, events listed live and checked against the loaded schema; custom scalars that declare @specifiedBy are checked by it.
- Suites: Run options (wait between steps 0-60 s, 1-100 runs, stop at the first failure), carried by Export as CI config and overridden by the CLI's --delay-ms, --bail and --iterations. Collections and folders can pin a Default environment.
- MCP control (off by default): an AI agent you run locally can drive RequestFox through `requestfox-mcp --http <port> --control` (21 extra tools: recording, calls, replay, send, mock and fail rules, profiles, saved requests and suites, exports, clear log, delete collection; throttle is Chrome only). RequestFox runs no AI model. One-time pairing code, 127.0.0.1 only, never the cookie jar, vault, secret variables or OAuth tokens; sending, replaying, deleting and clearing wait for the user's click; at most 120 tool calls a minute.
- Capture options: record the same site in other browser windows (opt-in) and Show page files (scripts, styles, images, fonts; off by default).
- Search: free text, field tokens such as status:500 and host:api.example.com, and a leading "-" to leave matching requests out.
- Testing: replay or edit-and-replay captured requests; compose requests with environments, {{variables}}, auth helpers (Bearer, Basic, Digest, API key, OAuth 2.0 with PKCE and device code, OAuth 1.0a, JWT Bearer signing, AWS Signature v4, HMAC) and saved collections, sent through the page with its own cookies while recording, or from the extension itself (no page cookies) when nothing is recording or the page's CORS blocks it; chain saved requests into suites with pass/fail per step and data-driven runs. Pre-request and post-response scripts run in Chrome only, in a sandbox.
- Mocking and rules: rules that make a matching endpoint fail, slow down, pause for editing, or return a chosen status and body, without backend changes. Rule profiles and mock sets stay on with nothing recording (optional site access, asked per profile or set). In Chrome, rewrite the request or the reply with a script; WebSocket message rules drop or change text messages (Chrome and Firefox). In Chrome, Slow down the whole tab (Slow 3G, Fast 3G, 4G, offline or custom) uses the optional debugger permission and shows Chrome's own debugging bar.
- Cookie jar: per site, off until turned on, for the requests RequestFox itself sends; the browser's own cookies are never sent or changed, and cookie values are never exported or logged. Importing the browser's cookies for a site asks for an optional cookies permission.
- Protocols: the QUERY method; gRPC-Web and Connect with the user's own .proto files (own parser); SOAP with WSDL import (including schemas split over files) and an XML tree.
- Import: Postman Collection v2.0/v2.1, Insomnia, Bruno, Hoppscotch, Thunder Client, OpenAPI 3, Swagger 2, HAR, cURL, WSDL and .env files; from a file, several files or a folder (batch import with one summary), or Import from URL (the browser asks for access to that one site).
- Export: self-contained HTML report, HAR, CSV, session JSON, Postman Collection, OpenAPI 3.0, code in 15 languages (cURL for bash and Windows cmd, PowerShell, fetch, Node.js, Python, HTTPie, Go, Java, C#, PHP, Ruby, Swift, Kotlin, Rust); Playwright and Cypress tests; GitHub and Linear issues pre-filled with a Markdown repro; collections for Bruno, Insomnia and Hoppscotch (secrets become empty variables); the saved collections as one API docs page (Export docs, HTML, no script).
- Examples and notes: save an answer as an example; notes on requests, collections and folders.
- Advice: caching and compression advice on answers, and a check that an answer stays the same as last time.
- WebSocket client: connects to any ws:// or wss:// server, with a Socket.IO mode.
- MCP server tester: Compose connects to an MCP server over Streamable HTTP (MCP 2026-07-28, and 2025 servers through initialize), lists its tools, resources and prompts, and calls one from a form built from its input schema. RequestFox contains no AI model and no AI code: it only sends the JSON-RPC requests the user picks and shows the answers; a server's request for a model completion is declined.
- LLM calls: a call whose answer is OpenAI-style, Anthropic or Gemini shows the model, the token counts and the stop reason that answer itself gives; no cost estimates. Like the MCP tester, it only tests and inspects other services.
- Command line (Node, one file, downloaded from the panel): assert (checks), diff, conform (traffic vs an OpenAPI spec), probe (negative tests made from an OpenAPI spec, sent to a local API), mock (a local mock API from a spec or a session; --dynamic varies answers, --seed repeats them), loadtest; docs (the API docs page from a workspace folder); explain (why a finding code is flagged); device-login (OAuth device code); --http2 on assert, diff, loadtest, run and probe (no quiet fall-back to HTTP/1.1; HTTP/3 is out of scope); --cookie-jar and --baseline (fail only on new findings); JUnit output.
- Load testing: generates k6, JMeter (.jmx), Gatling (.scala) and Locust (.py) scripts from a recorded session, using each endpoint's measured p95 latency as its threshold.
- Privacy: no account, no analytics, no telemetry; Authorization headers, cookies, secret-shaped fields and the page address are redacted by default in views and exports; site access is requested only when recording starts, or for the sites involved when Compose sends or a test suite runs with nothing recording.
- Languages: 14 (English, Arabic, German, Spanish, French, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese (Brazil), Russian, Turkish, Chinese (Simplified)).
- Compared with the Chrome DevTools Network panel: DevTools lists every resource live, throttles the whole page with nothing to allow, and leaves the judging to the user; RequestFox flags problems automatically, keeps session history for comparing runs, and supports checks and mock rules. Both show an open stream's events live; RequestFox also judges them and keeps them in History.
- Compared with Postman and Bruno: RequestFox covers composing requests, environments and collections, and additionally captures the real calls a web app makes in the browser. While recording it sends through the page; with nothing recording, Compose sends from the extension directly, like a standalone client; when an API blocks the page's origin (CORS), Compose can send from the extension instead, after a click, using the site access allowed at Start and without the page's cookies, a step standalone clients do not need. It has no cloud workspace or team sync. It exports collections for Bruno, Insomnia and Hoppscotch.
- Compared with Insomnia and Hoppscotch: both are API clients you build requests in (Insomnia a desktop app with plugins and Local Vault, Git or cloud storage; Hoppscotch on the web, desktop or CLI, self-hostable, with Socket.IO and MQTT clients). RequestFox records the calls a web app makes and flags problems; it imports collections from both and exports for both. RequestFox has no MQTT client.
- Compared with Requestly: Requestly offers a wider set of always-on traffic rules (redirects, script injection); RequestFox focuses on judging the calls (flags, checks, timing, the code and click behind each call).

The full text of every page, in one file: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/llms-full.txt

## Product

- [RequestFox: API Tester & Network Monitor, Chrome and Firefox](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/): Free API tester and network monitor for Chrome and Firefox: records your app's API calls, flags failed, slow and duplicate ones, replays and mocks them.
- [About RequestFox and AccessiSight](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/about.html): Who makes RequestFox, why it is free, and where your data lives: in your own browser, with no RequestFox server, no account and no analytics.
- [API Testing Extension FAQ: Chrome and Firefox · RequestFox](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/faq.html): Straight answers about testing APIs in the browser: which tool fits, finding failed or slow calls, GraphQL errors in a 200, mocking, exports and privacy.
- [RequestFox Features: Capture, Flag, Mock and Test APIs](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/features.html): Everything RequestFox does in your browser: capture fetch, XHR, WebSocket and SSE, flag broken calls, replay, mock, rewrite, check contracts, export tests.

## Guides

- [How to Run API Checks in CI From Saved Requests](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-api-checks-in-ci.html): Export a RequestFox suite as a CI config, download the one-file command-line tool, and run your API checks in any pipeline with JUnit results. Node 18+.
- [Mock an API Response in Chrome: Extension, No Backend](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-mock-api-response.html): Return your own status, headers and body for any API call, or make it fail, slow down or pause, in Chrome or Firefox. No backend change, no proxy.
- [Check Real API Calls Against an OpenAPI Spec](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-openapi-contract-check.html): Link an OpenAPI 3 or Swagger 2 spec and see which live calls break it, which are not in it, and how much of the API you covered. In the browser or in CI.
- [How to Record API Calls in Chrome or Firefox](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-record-api-calls.html): Record every fetch, XHR, WebSocket and SSE call a website makes in Chrome or Firefox, with failed and slow calls flagged. Step by step, free, no account.
- [How to Replay and Edit an API Request in Chrome](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-replay-edit-request.html): Resend a captured API request as it was, or change its method, URL, headers or body first, right in Chrome or Firefox. With the page's own cookies.
- [Guides: Record, Replay, Mock and Test APIs · RequestFox](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guides.html): Step-by-step guides: record API calls in Chrome, replay and edit requests, mock responses, check calls against OpenAPI, and run API checks in CI.

## Compare

- [RequestFox vs Bruno: In-Browser or Git-Native API Client](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-bruno.html): Bruno keeps API requests as plain files in Git; RequestFox starts from what your web app sends in the browser. Neither needs an account. When each fits.
- [RequestFox vs Chrome DevTools Network Panel](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-devtools.html): A Chrome DevTools Network alternative for API testing? What the Network panel does well, what RequestFox adds, and when to use each. Sourced, dated.
- [RequestFox vs Hoppscotch: Two Ways to Test APIs Online](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-hoppscotch.html): Hoppscotch is an open-source API client you can self-host; RequestFox records and judges the calls your own web app makes. Sourced from each tool's docs.
- [RequestFox vs Insomnia: Browser Extension or Desktop Client](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-insomnia.html): Insomnia is a desktop client for designing and testing APIs; RequestFox is a browser extension that flags what your web app really sends. Where each fits.
- [RequestFox vs Postman: A Postman Alternative Extension](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-postman.html): Looking for a Postman alternative in the browser? Postman suits team workspaces; RequestFox records and flags what your web app sends. Sourced, dated.
- [RequestFox vs Postman, DevTools, Insomnia, Bruno, Hoppscotch](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare.html): Which API tool fits which job: RequestFox compared with Postman, the DevTools Network panel, Insomnia, Bruno and Hoppscotch, with RequestFox's own limits.

## For

- [For API Developers: See How Clients Really Call Your API](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/use-api-developers.html): Watch the real calls a web client makes to your API, catch contract drift against your OpenAPI spec, and turn traffic into checks, CI runs and load tests.
- [For Frontend Developers: Debug the API Calls Your UI Makes](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/use-frontend-developers.html): See which component made each call, catch N+1 bursts and double fetches, mock the states you need, and check timing, without leaving the browser.
- [API Testing for QA Testers: Catch What the UI Hides](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/use-qa-testers.html): For manual and exploratory testers: see the API calls behind every click, catch failed, slow and duplicate requests, and attach evidence to bug reports.

## Optional

- [RequestFox Changelog: What's New in Each Release](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/changelog.html): What changed in each RequestFox release, newest first: new features, fixes and changes to the Chrome and Firefox extension, from its own changelog.
- [RequestFox Privacy Policy](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/privacy.html): RequestFox does not collect, transmit or sell any data. Everything it captures stays in your browser, on your device.
